chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When a man is struck on his head and his tongue becomes heavy, the letters of the alphabet are presented to him. He reads, then the wergild (blood money) is divided among the letters of the alphabet. Whatever he cannot pronounce clearly with his speech, the wergild is quantified based on that.

key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: Wergild or blood money paid for injury or death
key_terms.حُرُوفُ الْمُعْجَمِ: The letters of the Arabic alphabet

ai.seo_question: How is blood money calculated for head injuries affecting speech in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details a unique juristic methodology for assessing *diyah* (blood money) for head trauma resulting in speech impediments, where compensation is proportional to the specific letters of the Arabic alphabet the victim cannot articulate clearly. It reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of linking linguistic precision to physical injury, treating the alphabet as a measurable unit of functional loss. This approach underscores the importance of articulate speech in Islamic legal valuation of bodily harm.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al Halby, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘When the man is struck upon his head, so his tongues becomes heavy, the letters of the alphabet would be presented to him. He would read, then the wergild would be divided upon the letters of the alphabet. So whatever he could not pronounce eloquently with the speech, the wergild would be quantified by the measurement from that’.
